doc.title: Tom Scott interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 1, 2022 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Whitney Houston's phone call after his solo on her record
summary: Producer Michael Masser had him do many takes; Whitney Houston later phoned to thank him.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them

blocks.x: Were there sessions where you left after playing multiple solos and you didn’t know what they were going to use and you might not find out what they were going to use until you were in your car listening?

Every one, where I did multiple solos. I never knew what they were going to use. You’ve reminded me of a gentleman named Michael Masser. I can’t remember whether he’s still with us or not but he was a songwriter and record producer who called me one time, I didn’t know him but he got my number and said, “Listen I’m producing a new young lady. I think she’s a fantastic singer, I think she’s going to be a big star. Her name is Whitney Houston. And I’ve written a bunch of songs for her and I’d like you to play on one.” I said, “Fine.” So I showed up to the studio. Michael was there, Whitney Houston was not, she had already laid down her vocal tracks so she didn’t have to be there. And so it was a tune, it sort of reminded me, it definitely had a sort of 50s Doo-Wop kind of a feel. I mean it was a big production but basically was [scats] — that kind of a thing. So that’s nice, you know, pleasant. And so I played fills behind her and Michael Masser he kept wanting, “Oh well let’s do one more, do one more.” So I don’t know how many takes I did. It might have been over twenty. And finally I said, “Look, Michael, I don’t — whatever I did, whatever the best thing I could possibly do is, you’ve got it there somewhere. I don’t have any more to give to this thing. I’m done.” And I just said, “I have to go now.” So of course the record came out, it was a huge hit and I have some nice solos, things I’m very happy about. I think it enhanced the tune very well for what it was, you know tenor sax solo thing. About three months later, this is before the record came out the phone rings and I answer the phone, “Hello?” And a young lady says, “Is this Tom Scott?” I said, “Yes.” “Well you don’t know me but my name is Whitney Houston.

You played on my record.” And I had to think a minute. “Oh yeah, yeah, right, hi, yes, how are you?” And she said, “I just wanted you to know that I really really loved the work you did on my record.” And I said, “Well thank you, how nice of you to call, thanks for taking the time to do that.” That was about the end of the conversation. And you know with all the things that happened to Whitney Houston since then, unfortunate things, tragic things obviously, I’ve always — whenever I hear anything said about her kind of negative I go, “You know what? I’ve got to tell you something.” And look, I don’t expect people to do what she did. That was way beyond the call of duty as far as I’m concerned. But she took the time to get my phone number, pick up the phone, call me and tell me that. That’s a real kind gesture I think. And so I’ve always defended her saying look, and I always tell that story. And how many people do that? For whatever happened to her later in life she definitely was a kindhearted person, you know, in her heart.
Oh thank you for sharing that. It helps me look at her differently also.
